artwork.title: Frieze of Archers
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Jastrow, 2007, via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

lessons.title: Guards made of glazed brick

n1.text: Four archers march in step, two on each side of an inscription of King Darius in three languages. Every figure is built of small glazed bricks.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Run your eye along the four spears. Then compare the patterns on their robes: are any two the same?

q1.text: What are these bricks made of?

b1a.text: Not ordinary clay: a hard, white body under a glaze.

correction.truth: They are glazed siliceous ceramic: a white, very hard body coated with a brilliant glaze.

b1b.text: Not stone: each figure is built of bricks.

correction.tempting: The colours look as hard as stone.
correction.truth: Each brick was moulded, not carved, and glazed: a white siliceous body under a shiny coat.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Marcel Dieulafoy (1893); Jane Dieulafoy (1888).

b1c.text: Yes. The Louvre calls it glazed siliceous ceramic. The excavator described a white, very hard body under a brilliant glaze.

n2.text: Marcel Dieulafoy's French mission found these bricks at Susa in 1884–86, on the mound called the Apadana.

q2.text: How were the bricks lying when they were found?

correction.truth: The bricks were scattered, and almost all had been reused in later buildings.
correction.evidence: Marcel Dieulafoy (1893); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

b2b.text: Yes. They lay in heaps, and almost all the decorated bricks had been reused in later buildings. The archers were pieced together from them.

b2c.text: Nothing was neat: the bricks were mixed up.

correction.tempting: Each brick seems to fit perfectly in place.
correction.truth: They lay in tangled heaps, and most had been reused in later buildings.
correction.evidence: Marcel Dieulafoy (1893); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

n3.text: Darius wrote that many peoples built his palace at Susa. Babylonians moulded the bricks; Ionians and Sardians cut the stone.

q3.text: Who adorned the walls, according to Darius?

b3a.text: Yes. Darius says the men who adorned the wall were Medes and Egyptians. He does not say who made these particular bricks.

b3b.text: He names Ionians, but as stonecutters.

correction.tempting: Darius names Ionians among his workers.
correction.truth: Ionians and Sardians cut the stone; Medes and Egyptians adorned the wall.
correction.evidence: Kent's edition of Darius's inscription (1953); Encyclopaedia Iranica.

b3c.text: He names other peoples for this work.

correction.tempting: It was a Persian king's palace.
correction.truth: Darius names Medes and Egyptians as the men who adorned the wall.
correction.evidence: Kent's edition of Darius's inscription (1953); Encyclopaedia Iranica.

n4.text: In 1886 the excavators thought the archers were the 'Immortals': the ten thousand royal guards described by the Greek historian Herodotus.

correction.tempting: Their spears and jewels seemed to match Herodotus.
correction.truth: The Louvre's 1992 catalogue calls the identification speculative; Schmitt says it is far from proven.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

b4b.text: Yes. The idea goes back to the excavators. Later scholars call it speculative, far from proven. The Louvre's label calls them simply archers.

b4c.text: Their dress is Persian, not Greek.

correction.tempting: Herodotus, who described the Immortals, was Greek.
correction.truth: They wear Persian dress. Whether they are the Immortals is unproven.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

n6.text: The bricks went to Paris. By the early 1890s the archers, restored, were on show in the Louvre, set inside a border.

q5.text: Where did the restorers find the model for the panel's layout?

b5a.text: Not the inscription: they borrowed from another frieze.

correction.tempting: Darius's inscription describes how his palace was built.
correction.truth: The restored frame copies the border round Susa's lion frieze, also found by the Dieulafoys.
correction.evidence: Marcel Dieulafoy (1893); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

b5b.text: Not Herodotus: they borrowed from another frieze.

correction.tempting: The excavators matched the archers to Herodotus's royal guards.
correction.truth: The restored frame copies the border round Susa's lion frieze, also found by the Dieulafoys.
correction.evidence: Marcel Dieulafoy (1893); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

b5c.text: Yes. Marcel Dieulafoy reused his reconstruction of the border round the lions. The Louvre's 1992 catalogue says the modern restoration took the lion frieze as its model.

n7.text: Archers were only one subject. Darius's glazed walls at Susa also showed lions, griffins, winged bulls and sphinxes.

q6.text: Look at their dark brown skin. Did every guard at Susa look like this?

choices.label: No: guards came in two skin colours
No: each face was painted from life

b6a.text: Yes. Susa's guards were made in two conventional skin colours. The excavator found a hand moulded like the dark ones but glazed white: same mould, different glaze.

b6b.text: Not all alike: there were two colours.

correction.tempting: All four archers here share one skin colour.
correction.truth: Susa's guards came in two conventional skin colours; a white-glazed hand was made in the same mould as the dark ones.
correction.evidence: Jane Dieulafoy's diary (1888); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

b6c.text: Not portraits: the colours were set by convention.

correction.tempting: No two robes here share a pattern, so faces might differ too.
correction.truth: Skin came in two conventional colours, not portraits: a white hand was made in the same mould as the dark ones.
correction.evidence: Jane Dieulafoy's diary (1888); the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

n5.text: Bricks from a king's palace, scattered and pieced together again. The archers stand in Room 307, on Floor 0 of the Sully wing.

lessons.takeaway: Four archers in glazed brick from Darius I's palace at Susa, pieced together from scattered bricks in a frame copied from the lion frieze: Darius says Medes and Egyptians adorned his walls, the guards came in two conventional skin colours, and whether they are Herodotus's 'Immortals' is still unproven.
